# Three Empties {#sec-empties}

The first good hypothesis in the notebook was slightly too wide, and the
next calls retired the extra width. That is the experiment working.

The hypothesis, paraphrased from the comments: any genuinely empty thing
is the same immortal `NILSXP` cell. `NULL`, `c()`, and `pairlist()`
confirmed it, including under the strictest `identical()` switches, and
including `extptr.as.ref = TRUE`. Same address. Same type code 0. `REF`
pinned at the ceiling.

Then `list()` and `alist()` printed a different address, type 19,
`VECSXP`, length 0, empty flag bracket. Then `integer()`, `character()`,
`double()`, `logical()`, `complex()`, and `raw()` each printed a
zero-length vector of their own type. The hypothesis that survived is
sharper than the one that was written down first.

| Expression | SEXPTYPE | The Nil cell? | `typeof` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `NULL`, `c()`, `pairlist()` | `NILSXP` | yes, the only one | `"NULL"` |
| `list()`, `alist()` | `VECSXP`, length 0 | no | `"list"` |
| `integer()`, `character()`, … | a typed vector, length 0 | no | `"integer"`, `"character"`, … |

Untyped *pairlist* emptiness collapses. Every other zero is a real node of
its own type.

## Why Nil gets to be the only one

[R Internals](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-ints.html#The-data)
says there is only one object of type `NILSXP`, and it has no data. The
constructor in `memory.c` is worth reading slowly:

```c
/* R_NilValue */
/* THIS MUST BE THE FIRST CONS CELL ALLOCATED */
/* OR ARMAGEDDON HAPPENS. */
GET_FREE_NODE(R_NilValue);
SET_REFCNT(R_NilValue, REFCNTMAX);
SET_TYPEOF(R_NilValue, NILSXP);
CAR0(R_NilValue) = R_NilValue;
CDR(R_NilValue) = R_NilValue;
TAG(R_NilValue) = R_NilValue;
ATTRIB(R_NilValue) = R_NilValue;
MARK_NOT_MUTABLE(R_NilValue);
```

It is a cons cell that points at itself in every direction, allocated
before any other cons cell, with the reference count pinned and mutation
forbidden. The write barrier refuses assignments into its fields. Empty
hash buckets point at it. The empty formal list points at it. The end of
every pairlist points at it. "No binding here," "no attribute," "no rest
of this chain," and "the user said NULL" are the same node because the
Lisp tradition this evaluator comes from treats the empty list and nil as
one object, and because having two of them would make every `== R_NilValue`
pointer check a lie.

That is the sense in which Nil is special. Special does not mean "has a
richer identity than a typed empty." It means the runtime has exactly one,
forever, and a large amount of C code compares pointers against it. A
typed empty is special in a different way: it is allowed to be nothing of
a particular kind. Programs should imitate the second kind. A zero that
still has a type is a value you can pass through `lapply`, attach a name
to, and refuse to confuse with "the argument was missing."

## Why `list()` refuses to collapse

The tempting explanation is dispatch. `.S3PrimitiveGenerics` and
`.internalGenerics` are right there in the notebook, and they look like a
reason. They are a reason that some operations on vectors are wired into
the primitive table for speed. They are not why the empty list has its own
node.

`list()` is a {{< glossary "generic vector" >}}. The manual's description
of `VECSXP` is a header, a length, a true length, and a block of `SEXP`
pointers. Length zero is a legitimate block. It has to be, because the
zero of the user-facing heterogeneous container has to remain that
container:

- `typeof(list())` is `"list"`, and `length(list())` is 0
- `is.null(list())` is `FALSE`, which a huge amount of real code depends on
- you can set `names` on it, grow it with `[[<-`, and hand it to `lapply`
- an empty list with no class is still not `NULL`, so the `OBJ` bit and
  the class attribute stay out of the explanation

Pairlists follow the other rule because they are cons chains. The empty
chain *is* nil. `pairlist()` with no arguments returns `R_NilValue`. R
kept that rule for the substrate --- formals, attributes, the tail of a
call --- and grew a different empty for analysts.

`alist()` is the subtle one. An alist is a list that can hold missing
arguments; it is still a generic vector, not a pairlist. Empty, it is
another zero-length `VECSXP`, at its own address. The name "alist" is
historical. The representation is the vector world's.

## Typed emptiness is a value

`integer()` is not "nothing." It is a length-zero integer vector. Sum it,
recycle it, bind it as a column, give it a class. `character()` is a
length-zero `STRSXP`, which means a vector of `CHARSXP` pointers with no
pointers in it. The R-level word is `"character"`. The C-level word is
`STRSXP`. The single string inside a character vector is the thing called
`CHARSXP`, and you almost never hold one of those at R level. The notebook
guessed `STRSEXP`. Close, and the distinction matters the moment you read
a header.

`numeric()` is `double()` by another door. `typeof(numeric())` is
`"double"`. There is no `NUMSXP`.

This is also why `c()` with no arguments is Nil rather than "an empty
atomic vector of unknown type." `c()` is the concatenator. Given nothing
to concatenate and no type to inherit, it returns `NULL`. Given integers,
it returns an integer vector. The empty call is the degenerate case of a
function, not the zero of a type. `integer()` is the zero of a type. They
answer different questions, and the dumps are the proof that R refuses to
pretend they are the same question.

## What people mean by "no scalars"

S took a shortcut that still defines the language. Chambers describes it
in the
[2020 R Journal piece](https://journal.r-project.org/articles/RJ-2020-028/):
there were not enough hands to build a language with scalars and also
vectors, and the Fortran libraries underneath already thought in arrays.
So the low-level scalar work stayed on the other side of the interface,
and R inherited a world in which `1L` is an integer vector of length one.
The `scalar` bit in the header is an optimization for that common case,
not a new type.

Typed emptiness is the dual of that decision. If everything is a vector,
the empty vector has to exist, per type, or "zero of these" collapses into
"absence" and absence already has a resident. Nil is absence. `integer()`
is a count of zero. Keeping them apart is one of the few places R is
stricter than its reputation.
